newsitem.title: USA: Closing arguments in Reynolds case set for Friday.
newsitem.headline: Closing arguments in Reynolds case set for Friday.

text.p: After four weeks of often conflicting testimony and evidence, jurors hearing a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. are on the verge of a decision that could have wide implications for the tobacco industry.

Reynolds rested its defense Thursday. With no 11th-hour settlement in sight, the six-member jury will be asked to decide between plaintiff Dana Raulerson's contention that Reynolds made a dangerous product and should have to pay for it and Reynolds' claim that Raulerson's sister, the late Jean Connor, chose to smoke despite knowing the potential health risks involved.
For the first time in a Florida tobacco liability case, Connor's family will ask the jury not only to compensate it for her loss but to impose punitive damages against the company.

Closing arguments were expected to take at least five hours beginning Friday morning, with deliberations to follow. If the jurors do not reach a decision Friday, they will return to the task Monday morning, having told Judge Bernard Nachman they were not willing to work over the weekend.

The lawsuit was filed by the family of Connor, a heavy smoker who took up cigarettes as a teen-ager and developed a three-pack-a-day habit through 35 years of smoking before she succumbed to lung cancer in October 1995. She was 49.

Connor, who said she was addicted and knew she was dying, filed a product liability lawsuit against Reynolds, the manufacturers of Salem, her favorite brand, before she died. After her death, her sister took up the cause, refiling the action on behalf of Connor's estate.

Raulerson's attorney is Norwood "Woody" Wilner, a lawyer in private practice in Jacksonville who last year won a $750,000 judgment for client Grady Carter of Orange Park, Fla., an air traffic controller who alleged he contracted lung cancer from a lifetime of smoking.
Yet on the eve of closing arguments Thursday, with the tobacco litigation field watching to see if he can do it again, Wilner played down the potential impact of another win.
"I don't know if it has to be a favorable verdict. I think the message has already been sent," Wilner said. "Everyone knows that the industry must take these cases seriously.
"They may win or they may lose, but they can't ignore these cases. They are coming," he said.
Wilner said he was open to a last-minute settlement offer, but none had been made. "My phone is on the hook. They haven't called," he said.

The judgment in the Carter case last August against Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp., a unit of Britain's B.A.T Industries Plc, was only the second time a monetary award had been made against a tobacco company. The first, a $400,000 judgment won by the family of Rose Cipollone of New Jersey in 1988, was overturned on appeal and the case eventually was dropped.
The tobacco industry declared the Carter judgment an aberration. The case is being appealed.

But another victory for Wilner, tobacco litigation experts have said, could speak volumes about a changing tide against tobacco companies, which for decades have denied they were marketing a product that had been proven dangerous.

The industry has suffered some serious setbacks of late, including last week's court ruling that the Food and Drug Administration can regulate tobacco as a drug, and cigarette maker Liggett Group's recent offer to settle state lawsuits.

In an April 29 newsletter to investors, New York-based tobacco industry analyst Gary Black of Bernstein Research called the Raulerson case a barometer "as to whether jurors, in the face of all this negative publicity, will award money to smokers who become ill."
He said the most likely outcome was a hung jury, which would be seen as a "huge win" for the industry.
During the trial, jurors heard conflicting testimony on what killed Connor and what role smoking played in her death.

They saw company documents, including a controversial 1962 Reynolds paper in which a senior researcher, Alan Rodgman, said the amount of evidence accumulated to indict cigarette smoking as a health hazard was "overwhelming."

They also got a brief glimpse of Connor herself, bald from chemotherapy, frail and gaunt on videotape in the days before her death. It was a startling vision that so affected Judge Nachman that he ordered the tape halted and edited down to a minute, fearing more would prejudice the jury.
